title: Time pressure and thriving: why learning, vitality, and engagement should remain separate
question: Does job control determine whether daily time pressure relates positively or negatively to learning, vitality, engagement and exhaustion?

# Time pressure and thriving: why learning, vitality, and engagement should remain separate

Narrative review draft (v2, full-text appraised) · not submission-ready · 9 October 2026

## Review question

Under which measured conditions are time pressure and work resources associated with different components of employee experience?

Focus confirmed by the author on 9 October 2026 ([decisions](question-decisions.md)).

## Evidence base and method

The author's folder (`Paper 19 Nov 2024/References/156TMIEOC`) holds 75 PDFs. Sixty-nine were identified against Crossref, including one diary study identified by hand from its title page (Kühnel et al., 2012, 10.1111/j.2044-8325.2011.02022.x). None is retracted. Forty-seven were excluded (`screening.json`):

- 40 use "time" in another sense, such as presenteeism over time, shopping time or team performance over time
- 6 books without a text layer
- 1 duplicate PDF

The 28 included studies measure **time pressure** (12), **working-time demands and control** such as overtime, schedule autonomy, commutes and care time (11), or resources and daily experience without either (5). They were coded for resources tested, outcome components and design (`coding.json`). Eight use day- or week-level designs [R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8]. Quotes were checked against the cited PDF pages.

## What the collection shows

### 1. Time pressure has no single sign; its association depends on measured conditions

The time-pressure studies agree on one thing: time pressure is neither uniformly good nor uniformly bad. They identify the conditions under which its sign changes:

- **Job control (day level).** "on days with higher job control, time pressure was beneficial for work engagement. On days with lower job control, time pressure was detrimental for work engagement" [R1, abstract].
- **Dose and task legitimacy.** The study found "an inverted U-shape relation between time pressure and work engagement". The motivating effect of moderate time pressure held "only when employees are assigned to tasks with a low unreasonability rating" [R9, abstract].
- **The qualitative source of the pressure.** Controlling for qualitative challenge demands, "time pressure positively related to exhaustion, but negatively related to work engagement and self-esteem" [R5, abstract]. Whether time pressure looks like a challenge depends on which co-occurring demands are held constant.
- **The employee's appraisal.** Employees who appraised time pressure and job complexity as challenges "reported higher job satisfaction and work engagement and felt less emotionally exhausted" than those with dominant hindrance or threat appraisals. Resilience and autonomy predicted the challenge profile [R10, abstract].

The common lesson is that a study reporting "the effect of time pressure" without the moderating condition (control, legitimacy, accompanying demands or appraisal) reports an average over opposite processes.

### 2. Learning and vitality respond differently, so thriving should not be one score

A diary study of 124 knowledge workers found that challenge stressors (time pressure and learning demands) "have a positive total effect on learning but no total effect on vitality" [R2, PDF p1]. The paths differed: effects on learning ran through challenge appraisal, while learning demands affected vitality through hindrance appraisal [R2, abstract]. The authors concluded: "These differential relationships call for a ﬁner distinction between the two components of thriving at work" [R2, PDF p1].

Engagement and exhaustion also diverge within the same study [R5]. A single combined "employee experience" score would hide these opposing associations.

### 3. Within-person timing reveals reciprocal and lagged effects

Week-level data show time pressure as both cause and consequence. Over three weeks, "a positive lagged effect of PWB in the ﬁrst week on experiencing time pressure in the second week; in turn, time pressure in the second week had a negative lagged effect on PWB in the third week" [R3, PDF p1]. Time pressure also *facilitated* action on days of low positive affect, reducing procrastination [R6, abstract]. Its function depends on the person's state that day.

Spillover beyond work is measured too. Time pressure predicted seeking spousal support, with gender-specific spillover and crossover patterns among 308 dual-earner couples [R11, abstract].

### 4. Working-time demands and control: autonomy helps, but with limits

Large panel studies assess working-time arrangements rather than felt pressure:

- In 4,019 German workers over 16,076 person-years, "Changing to or remaining in autonomous working-time arrangements had a positive effect on job satisfaction" [R12, abstract]. The study used working excessive hours as a threshold moderator.
- A three-wave representative panel (n = 3,390) tested whether work-time control reduces exhaustion through internal work–home interference, including reversed and reciprocal paths [R13, abstract].

These designs are stronger for causal ordering than single surveys. They measure objective arrangements, not the felt time pressure of the diary studies, so the two literatures answer different questions.

## Conclusions this collection supports

1. **Report time-pressure effects only with their conditions.** Job control [R1], task legitimacy and dose [R9], co-occurring demands [R5] and appraisal [R10] each change the sign or size of the association.
2. **Keep components separate.** Learning ≠ vitality [R2], and engagement ≠ exhaustion [R5]. Combining them can cancel real effects.
3. **Model time pressure as dynamic.** Lagged and reciprocal within-person effects [R3] and state-dependent functions [R6] mean single-occasion designs miss the process.
4. **Distinguish felt pressure from working-time arrangements.** Panel evidence on autonomy [R12, R13] and diary evidence on felt pressure address different constructs.

## Limits

- 28 included studies from one curated folder. Many are German or Western European diary studies from a small number of research groups, which may limit generalizability.
- Resource and outcome coding is from abstracts plus machine-copied Method passages. Effect sizes are not pooled.

## Proposed research direction

The companion protocol proposes a day-level diary study that measures time pressure with its source (legitimate vs. unreasonable tasks) and job control. It measures learning, vitality, engagement and exhaustion as separate outcomes, and lagged next-day effects. Pre-registered moderation tests correspond to sections 1 and 2. It remains a proposal pending population, access and ethics decisions.

# Paper 19 — Empirical protocol v2: Time pressure and thriving: conditions and separate components

> **Status: PROPOSAL awaiting AMET University Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) approval.** No data have been collected; no results exist. Sample sizes are computed from **assumed** smallest effects of interest, not from any study. Instruments are ScaleScope catalogue entries whose source articles were resolved on Crossref (9 October 2026). Version 2 replaces the v1 draft `paper-19-nov-2024-protocol.md`.

## 1. Research question
Does job control determine whether daily time pressure relates positively or negatively to learning, vitality, engagement and exhaustion?

## 2. Hypotheses (to be pre-registered)
- H1: Time pressure x job control interaction on daily engagement.
- H2: Time pressure relates positively to learning but not to vitality.
- H3: Today's time pressure predicts tomorrow's proactive behaviour (lagged).

## 3. Design
Baseline + 10-working-day diary, two surveys per day (midday, end of day).

**Measurement occasions**
- Baseline
- Days 1-10 x 2 surveys

## 4. Population, eligibility and recruitment
**Population(s):** a paid online research panel (Indian working adults); working professionals in India (organisations reached through alumni, professional networks and recruiter contacts).

**Eligibility:** Employed adults (18+), full-time. Exclusion: failing two or more embedded attention checks; incomplete primary measures at the analysed wave (handled under §8).

**Recruitment and independence safeguards**
- **Paid online panel** — a commercial panel provider (to be selected; must allow India-resident adult workers, pre-screening on eligibility, attention checks and payment at or above the provider's fair-pay guidance). Prescreen answers are re-asked inside the survey for verification.
- **Working professionals in India** — via alumni networks, professional associations and LinkedIn posts; where organisational data (HR records, supervisor ratings) are needed, a signed **organisational access letter / data-sharing agreement** is obtained first and the organisation never sees individual responses.

## 5. Measures

| Work design - autonomy | Work Design Questionnaire (WDQ, #196) | 53 | baseline and daily short form | [10.1037/0021-9010.91.6.1321](https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.91.6.1321) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |
| Thriving at work (learning, vitality) | Thriving at Work Scale (—, #55) | 10 | daily | [10.1002/job.756](https://doi.org/10.1002/job.756) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |

All instruments are administered in English (the working language of the target population). Any translation or wording adaptation (e.g. day-level or target-shifted versions) is labelled **adapted — not validated**, piloted with cognitive interviews (n ≈ 10) and checked for factor structure before the main study.

## 6. Sample size
Between-person associations: r = 0.3 needs 85 persons (80% power, two-sided α = .05); the target is set at **100 persons × 10 days** (≈1000 day-observations), the conventional floor for cross-level interactions. With assumed attrition/exclusion of 25% across waves, recruit **134**. *Assumption:* Persons sized for between-level r = .30; within-person interaction power by simulation.

Target completers: **100**; recruitment target: **134**. Power will be re-checked by simulation with pilot variances before pre-registration; if the target is not reachable, the study is reported as estimation (confidence intervals) rather than as a confirmatory test.

## 7. Procedure and timing
1. IEC approval → OSF pre-registration (hypotheses, analysis, exclusions, stopping rule) → pilot (n ≈ 30, not analysed for hypotheses).
2. Recruitment window ≈ 6 weeks per wave; two reminders per wave; reminders stop on withdrawal.
3. Waves linked by a self-generated pseudonymous code; the linking key is stored separately from responses.
4. Data collection ends when the recruitment target is met or the pre-registered end date passes, whichever is first.

## 8. Analysis plan
Multilevel models with person-mean-centred day predictors; lagged within-person effects.

- **Missing data:** full-information maximum likelihood (or multiple imputation, 20+ imputations) under MAR; attrition analysed against baseline variables and reported.
- **Measurement:** CFA for each multi-item measure; reliability (ω and α) reported; measurement invariance across waves/groups before comparing means or paths.
- **Inference:** two-sided α = .05; effect sizes with 95% CIs; Holm correction across the confirmatory hypothesis family; exploratory analyses labelled as such.
- **Common-method bias:** temporal separation and, where planned, other-source ratings; a marker variable is included in the survey.

## 9. Ethics (ICMR 2017 National Ethical Guidelines)
- **Risk category:** Minimal risk — request **expedited review**. Rationale: Questions about everyday work experiences; no deception, no intervention, no identifiable data published.
- **Consent:** written/electronic informed consent before any question; separate consent items for each optional element (record linkage, co-worker/supervisor contact, follow-up waves).
- **Voluntariness:** no penalty for non-participation or withdrawal; no data from or to supervisors/appraisers at individual level.
- **Confidentiality & data protection:** pseudonymised data, linking key held only by the PI on an encrypted drive; processing consistent with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; retention 5 years after publication (or as the IEC directs), then deletion.
- **Support:** debrief page with the national tele-mental-health helpline (Tele-MANAS, 14416 — verify before use) and contact details of the PI and IEC.
- Ethics pack (IEC application summary, participant information sheet, consent form, debrief): `../ethics/paper-19-nov-2024-ethics-pack.md`.

## 10. Open science
OSF pre-registration before data collection; de-identified data and analysis code shared on OSF after publication where consent permits (HR-record and organisational data excluded unless the organisation agrees).

**Why are we doing this study?** Our research question is: Does job control determine whether daily time pressure relates positively or negatively to learning, vitality, engagement and exhaustion?
